title: About me
text:
Hi, I’m James Lindsay (jimbo).
I’m the Director of Software Engineering and a bioinformatics engineer in the Department of Data Science at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.
My work sits at the intersection of cancer genomics, spatial biology, and clinical informatics. I spend my days building software and data infrastructure that translates massive genomic datasets into something clinicians can actually use to help patients.
Most notably, I helped architect MatchMiner, an open-source platform that automatically matches cancer patients to clinical trials based on their genomic profiles. I also led the development of ImmunoProfile, a machine-learning workflow that uses spatial data to understand the tumor immune microenvironment.
I’ve also built infrastructure for major national consortia like AACR Project GENIE and contribute to the cBioPortal.

title: How AI is Buying Back the Doctor-Patient Relationship
text:
A patient sits with their oncologist, absorbing the news that their cancer has progressed. They watch as the doctor tabs between a dense electronic medical record, a PDF of genetic test results, and a browser window open to ClinicalTrials.gov.
This scene plays out daily in cancer clinics, where the difference between a missed opportunity and a viable treatment often hinges on the limits of human processing power. The world’s knowledge is instantly searchable, yet clinical trial matching remains a painstaking, manual exercise. It is a search for a needle in a haystack where the needle is continually changing shape.
Clinical trial eligibility is expressed in dense, unstructured language that resists simple rules or checklists. A patient’s medical history is similarly fractured, with key details scattered among physician notes, pathology reports, and genomic tests. None of these were designed to be read by machines.
Seen this way, trial matching begins to look less like a clinical judgment problem and more like an information discovery problem. And that is exactly how computer scientists are now solving it. By pairing large language models with a paradigm known as “retrieve and re-rank,” researchers have built a system that allows doctors to search for trials using the most natural interface available: the patient’s own story.
On the everyday web, search problems are largely solved. You can search for “running shoes” on Amazon and instantly filter by size, color, and brand because products come with structured tags. But patients don’t have tags; they are biographies composed of their medical, cancer, and personal journeys. A patient’s history might describe symptoms of kidney failure using nuanced narrative language, which standard search tools miss unless a physician explicitly translates those stories into rigid database terms like “renal insufficiency.”
This “translation tax” is what breaks the workflow. Existing tools like ClinicalTrials.gov assume that clinicians will search for trials the way database administrators do: by translating clinical questions into structured queries and predefined fields. But in practice, physicians think in narrative, patient-centered terms. The burden of translating a complex clinical situation into the language of a database has long fallen on them, eating up the precious few minutes they have with the patient.
Timing is the critical variable. Often, the full picture of a patient’s health only coalesces when they are sitting in front of their care team. If a clinical trial is to be an option, the physician needs to know about it in that moment. They simply do not have the time to leave the room, summarize the patient’s history, translate it into database queries, and perform an exhaustive search.
When time is limited, the goal shifts. The priority is no longer to exhaustively prove a patient’s eligibility, but to rapidly surface the most plausible options. This is where the new “retrieve and re-rank” system steps in. By allowing the physician to input a natural language summary and focusing only on key eligibility criteria, the system reframes the task itself: from proving eligibility upfront to prioritizing which possibilities deserve closer human attention.
The arrival of Large Language Models (LLMs) seemed to offer an easy fix. In theory, a system like GPT-4 could read a patient’s file and reason through eligibility criteria just like a human. But researchers at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute quickly ran into a wall of simple arithmetic: scale. Deep reasoning models are computationally heavy. Asking an LLM to “read” thousands of open clinical trials against a complex patient history in real-time is computationally intractable and prohibitively slow.
To solve this, the Dana-Farber team took a page from the playbook of the world’s biggest search engines. They adopted a two-step architecture known as “retrieve and re-rank.” In this framing, the goal isn’t to have the AI make a final medical judgment, but to rapidly build a short list of high-quality candidates that the physician can review at a glance. This speed buys the physician agency. Because the results appear almost instantly, doctors don’t have to abdicate their responsibility to a black box. They maintain full narrative control, editing the patient summary to address missing data or late-breaking changes in real-time.
The mechanics of this discovery engine rely on a pipeline designed to balance speed with rigor. It begins with an act of compression. An LLM ingests the scattered fragments of a patient’s history—physician notes, pathology reports, genetic tests—and distills them into a concise “clinical summary.” Rather than a free-form story, this summary is a structured snapshot defined by key coordinates: cancer type, disease burden, biomarkers, age, and prior treatments. The system performs the same translation on every clinical trial in the database, breaking them down into the same fundamental components.
Once the patient and the trials speak the same language, the “Retrieve” phase begins. The system converts these text summaries into numerical representations called vector embeddings. This maps every patient and every trial to a specific point in a high-dimensional mathematical space.
To make this map useful, the researchers customized an open-source model using a technique called contrastive learning. By training the model on thousands of synthetically generated patient-trial pairs, they taught it the geometry of eligibility: adjusting the mathematical landscape so that a patient with a specific mutation lands in the same neighborhood as trials targeting that mutation, while pushing incompatible trials far away. This reliance on synthetic data solved a dual problem: it provided the massive volume of examples deep learning requires, while bypassing the privacy constraints that lock up real medical records.
Finally, the system moves to the “Re-rank” phase. Here, speed is traded for accuracy. A separate “text-classification” model—heavier and more computationally expensive—acts as the final judge. It reads the patient summary against the top 50 trial candidates one by one, performing a binary check: Is this patient eligible? Yes or No? Because this intense scrutiny is limited to only the most promising candidates, the system can deliver deep clinical reasoning in seconds rather than hours.
At the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, this theoretical engine has already entered the exam room. In a pilot program at affiliated community clinics, physicians have begun using the system as part of their daily rounds. They start not with a database query, but by reviewing a concise, AI-generated summary of the patient’s situation in plain English. The result is an instant, prioritized list of trials that serves as a starting point for the conversation.
The impact is best measured not in search metrics, but in relief. As one clinician in the pilot put it: “Please don’t take this away from me.” In the high-stakes, time-sensitive conversations between oncologists and patients, simply having credible options visible early enough to discuss them changes the nature of the appointment. It shifts the dynamic from a frantic search for data to a thoughtful consideration of choices.
Perhaps the most significant outcome of this engineering choice is that the tool is not locked behind a proprietary wall. Because the underlying models were trained entirely on synthetic data, they contain no private health information. This allows the researchers to release the models as open-source software, removing the financial barrier for hospitals globally. In a field where the slow pace of recruitment acts as a brake on all of medicine, democratizing access to discovery tools effectively hits the accelerator.
Yet, speed comes with its own shadows. The relevance of any AI suggestion is tethered to the data it sees, and there is a risk that a ranked list of trials might be treated with undue authority, subtly shaping a doctor’s judgment before they have even spoken to the patient. Systematic evaluation remains difficult; clinical workflows vary wildly from the academic halls of Dana-Farber to rural community clinics, and it remains an open question whether this digital efficiency will translate uniformly across the messy reality of global healthcare.
The goal is not to replace the physician’s judgment, but to unburden it. Back in the exam room, the oncologist finishes reviewing the AI-generated list and turns away from the screen. They swivel their chair to look the patient in the eye. “We have some promising options,” they say, “but before we dive into the details, I want to hear how you’re feeling.” In this moment, the machine’s role is finished. It has not made the decision, but it has quietly reshaped the space in which the decision takes form. It clears away the administrative noise so that the human connection can, once again, take center stage.

title: DO NOT MAKE DIRECT EDITS, ONLY MAKE SUGGESTIONS
text:
1. The Core Philosophy: “Accessible Rigor”
The Quanta mission is to “illuminate science.” Unlike general news outlets that focus on the implications of a discovery (e.g., “Will this cure cancer?”), Quanta focuses on the mechanism of the discovery (e.g., “How does the math actually work?”).

The Rule: Never hand-wave the hard part. If a concept is central to the story, it must be explained, no matter how abstract.
The Method: Use a “Ladder of Abstraction” to walk the reader from a simple, tangible metaphor up to the complex reality.

title: DO NOT MAKE DIRECT EDITS, ONLY MAKE SUGGESTIONS
text:
2. The Structural Formula (The 6-Part Arc)
Most long-form Quanta articles follow a specific six-part narrative arc.

Phase 1: The Hook (The “Paradox” or “Mystery”)
Quanta rarely starts with the breaking news. Instead, it starts with a broad, accessible entry point that establishes the stakes. * Technique: Open with a historical puzzle, a famous paradox, or a relatable scene. * Example: “Nearly 200 years ago, physicists wrote down equations for how fluids swirl. For 200 years, we thought they worked. We were wrong.”


Phase 2: The Nut Graf (The “Turn”)
Usually appearing in the 3rd or 4th paragraph, this is where the specific new discovery is introduced. It pivots the story from the broad history to the specific “News Hook.” * Key Phrase: “But now…” or “Then, last year…” or “In a paper released this week…” * Function: It connects the ancient mystery (Phase 1) to the new solution.


Phase 3: The Context (The “Deep Dive”)
Before explaining the new thing, the article pauses to explain the old thing. This is the “textbook” section where background concepts are taught. * The “Ladder” Technique: * Rung 1 (Metaphor): “Think of the universe like a rubber sheet…” * Rung 2 (Concept): “This is known as the curvature of spacetime.” * Rung 3 (Specifics): “In the new model, this curvature is calculated using…” * Goal: Ensure the reader understands the problem so they can appreciate the solution.


Phase 4: The Action (The “Quest”)
This section focuses on the narrative of the scientists themselves. It details the struggle, the dead ends, and the “Aha!” moment. * Narrative Tension: Science is framed as a battle against confusion. * Human Element: Quotes are used to show emotion (“We were stuck for years,” “It was a nightmare”), not just facts.


Phase 5: The Mechanics (The “Solution”)
This is the hardest part of the article: explaining the new discovery in detail. * Mechanistic Explanation: Instead of just stating the result, Quanta explains how it happens. * Bad: “The algorithm finds the error.” * Quanta: “The neural network freezes the fluid simulation in time, zooming in on the glitch until it becomes a static, manageable picture.” * Visual Integration: The text explicitly references diagrams or animations (“As seen in the video above…”) to do the heavy lifting.


Phase 6: The Outlook (The “Horizon”)
The conclusion rarely claims the problem is “solved.” Instead, it opens up a new mystery. * Tone: Cautious optimism. * Key Sentiment: “This is a major step, but the real work has just begun.”

title: DO NOT MAKE DIRECT EDITS, ONLY MAKE SUGGESTIONS
text:
3. The Stylistic Toolkit

A. Visual Metaphors
Quanta writers are masters of the concrete analogy. They map abstract mathematical objects onto physical things. * Examples: * Math: “Balancing a pen perfectly on its tip” (for unstable singularities). * Physics: “Like inflating a tire” (for expanding spacetime). * Biology: “Bullying” (for cells expelling weaker neighbors).


B. The “Personification of Ideas”
Mathematical entities are often treated as characters. Equations “struggle,” shapes “refuse to cooperate,” and variables “blow up.” This gives agency to abstract concepts, making them easier to follow.


C. “Time-Travel” Pacing
Articles often jump between centuries. A common pattern is connecting a 19th-century giant (Euler, Riemann, Darwin) directly to a modern PhD student. This validates the modern work by anchoring it in a grand lineage.

title: DO NOT MAKE DIRECT EDITS, ONLY MAKE SUGGESTIONS
text:
4. Tone & Voice

Authoritative but Humble: The voice is confident in the facts but cautious about the implications.
Precise: Exact terminology is used (e.g., “manifolds,” “quintessence”) but always defined.
Wonder-filled: There is an underlying sense of awe at the elegance of the universe.

title: DO NOT MAKE DIRECT EDITS, ONLY MAKE SUGGESTIONS
text:
5. Summary Checklist for Writers
If you want to write like Quanta: - [ ] Start with a mystery, not the result. - [ ] Identify the “Turn”: Where does the old knowledge end and the new discovery begin? - [ ] Build a Ladder: Start with a metaphor, end with the math. - [ ] Show the Struggle: Include quotes about the difficulty of the research. - [ ] Explain “How”: Don’t just say it works; explain the mechanism. - [ ] End with a Question: What is still unknown?

title: About me
text:
About this blog
I wanted to start writing casually for a long time but I’ve always struggled getting started. Through my profesesional career I’ve found academic writing to be exetremely challenging and time consuming and some inital attempts at “blogging” failed quickly. I tried again recently, this time relying heavily on AI tools to help with the writing. If I can successfully keep this going I’ll describe my process. In general the text on this page is mostly written by me but heavily edited by AI.
